title: A Canadian study pinned a baby's death on codeine passed through breast milk. 20 years on, it's been retracted

A highly influential yet controversial Canadian study that linked a baby's death to codeine passed through breastmilk — and informed global guidance on breastfeeding and pain management over the last two decades — has been pulled from a leading medical journal, which said omissions in the research amounted to "falsification."
Omissions amounting to 'falsification' identified in influential 2006 study, The Lancet journal medical says

A highly influential yet controversial Canadian study that linked a baby's death to codeine passed through breast milk — and informed global guidance on breastfeeding and pain management over the last two decades — has been pulled from a leading medical journal, which said omissions in the research amounted to "falsification."

In the latest issue of The Lancet, set for release Nov. 21, the journal announced it has retracted the 2006 paper by Gideon Koren, the once esteemed founder of the Motherisk drug testing lab at the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) in Toronto.

The saga involving Koren's long-questioned study included years of Canadian media coverage, a sweeping New Yorker investigation last January, and a decision by The Lancet to add an "expression of concern" to the case report in February following new allegations of falsified toxicological data, authorship issues and ethical concerns.
The case focused on the deadly poisoning of an Ontario infant in 2005.

The study purported that the boy's mother was prescribed the painkiller Tylenol 3, which contains both acetaminophen and codeine — a mild opioid that gets partially metabolized into morphine inside the body — causing a deadly amount of morphine to pass to the boy through her breast milk.

items: Why a 20-year-old study claiming a baby died from opioid poisoning through breast milk is still under fire

blocks.text: Koren long insisted the case showed maternally ingested codeine can be fatal for breastfeeding infants, despite mounting questions about that likelihood from other pediatricians and toxicologists.

"This paper is the cornerstone of an entire field of pediatric pharmacology and toxicology that, honestly, should not exist," said Toronto-based internist and pharmacologist Dr. David Juurlink, a longtime critic of what he called a "botched" study on a coroner's investigation.

"This isn't just about one mischaracterized infant death. The narrative that babies can die through opioids passed through breast milk has greatly influenced postpartum pain care. It has caused women taking opioids to forgo breastfeeding, thereby depriving infants of the benefits of breastfeeding, which are numerous."
Tainted Tests: Broken Families
'Omitted findings' in case report

The Lancet's retraction notice said the journal had received the "outcome and conclusion" of a formal investigation from SickKids' research integrity office after referring its allegations to the Toronto hospital.
"The authorship issues and ethical concerns could not be fairly investigated as a meaningful participation of Gideon Koren was unlikely to be possible," reads the notice.

"On the allegation of omission of material toxicological data, including the infant's blood codeine and acetaminophen concentrations and the qualitative identification of codeine in the infant's stomach contents, the report concluded that this omission constitutes falsification. The omitted findings left readers without the information necessary to assess the publication's conclusion."
It's just the latest blow against Koren, who relinquished his medical licence in Ontario after a scandal-filled career that included the closure of the Motherisk lab in 2019.

The facility gained worldwide attention for using hair strands to test for drug and alcohol use in mothers — methods deemed "inadequate and unreliable" by an independent provincial review in 2015, but not before they were used in thousands of child protection cases and broke apart families across the country.

blocks.text: CBC News has contacted Koren for comment.
In a statement to CBC News following The Lancet's retraction notice, a spokesperson for SickKids said the facility "takes all matters of research integrity seriously."

The hospital's formal inquiry concluded material toxicological data had been omitted from the published report and determined that this "constituted falsification under SickKids' Responsible Conduct of Research Policy." The hospital declined to provide further details on the findings, due to the "confidential nature of research integrity inquiries."

blocks.text: The Lancet's retraction notice has been "a long time coming," Juurlink said.

"It's surprising that it took such a long time for this to happen. Not just that it took a long time, but that it took investigative journalism to cast a light on the institutional failures that kept this paper alive for 20 years."
